# Water
Big cultural shifts are needed to protect Wisconsin’s water resources
Wisconsin industry, communities, plants, wildlife, and fisheries depend on the quality of our 84,000 miles of rivers and streams, 15,000 lakes, 5.3 million acres of wetlands, and groundwater resources. The Mississippi River and two Great Lakes, Lake Superior and Lake Michigan, border Wisconsin, providing 1,000 miles of Great Lakes coastline. These water resources add to our economy and provide unique natural resources. We are already seeing major impacts to these water resources because of climate change.
Read the full water report (pdf)

# Water
## Summary of the Issues
Warming temperatures and changing precipitation patterns are impacting water resources in Wisconsin. Ross Allen Lake, Vilas Co. Photo credit: Dea Larsen Converse

# Water
## Summary of the Issues
### Water Resources
Warming temperatures and changing precipitation patterns are leading to more harmful algal blooms, reduced water quality, changing aquatic ecosystems, loss of ice cover, alternating periods of flooding and drought. Despite these challenges, steps can and are being taken to make Wisconsin’s water resources more resistant and resilient. Our expectations and regulations for managing the areas around our lakes, rivers, and wetlands need to shift to accommodate this rapidly changing climate.

# Water
## Summary of the Issues
### Fisheries
Fishing is an important part of the culture and economy in Wisconsin. Lakes, streams, and rivers provide vital tribal subsistence, commercial, and recreational fisheries worth nearly $2 billion annually to the state. As water temperatures warm, the fish species that can live in our waters will change. More frequent extreme storms and heat events are already damaging fish habitat and stressing fisheries. These impacts will intensify as the climate continues to warm.

# Water
## Summary of the Issues
### Great Lakes
Wisconsin is bordered by two Great Lakes, Lake Superior to the north and Lake Michigan to the east. It is hard to overstate how influential the Great Lakes are to the region. They not only sup-port the local economy; they also greatly influence the weather. The area along the Great Lakes is warming faster than the general pattern of warming across the state, leading to physical changes to the Great Lakes that are already being felt. Water level fluctuations, changes to water temperature and lake mixing, and ice cover changes are impacting coastal land, habitats, water quality, and iconic species like walleye and wild rice.

# Water
## Summary of the Issues
### Mississippi River
Climate change is increasing variability in river flows in the Mississippi River. In high water years, the excessive volume of water damages infrastructure and significantly reduces the reliability of river transportation. Natural resources like aquatic plant populations, a critical food source for hundreds of thousands of migrating waterfowl, and floodplain forests have suffered. High water years also increase the delivery of sediment and nutrients to the river and backwater areas, which increases the prevalence of harmful algal blooms and contributes to the expansion of the Gulf of Mexico hypoxic zone.
> The risk to natural communities is particularly acute for tribes in northern Wisconsin. The wild rice beds, fish, and wildlife that are an important part of their culture and provide them with food security are stressed by the change in climate.

# Water
## Key Points
Life along the Great Lakes has always meant living with dynamic water conditions but climate change threatens more extremes in water level conditions in the future. Breaking Blue, 2016 Great Lakes Photo Contest, Cave Point County Park, Door County, Wisconsin. Photo credit: Michael Braaten

# Water
## Key Points
### Water Resources and Ecosystems Are Changing
Warming temperatures and changing precipitation patterns are decreasing water quality and changing aquatic ecosystems.

# Water
## Key Points
### Tribes Will Be Impacted
Warmer water temperatures and increasing variability in ice on and off dates, duration and thickness are changing the fish species that can live in Wisconsin’s waters. Cool- and cold-water fish are particularly at risk. Loss of these resources will have spiritual, cultural, and health impacts to Wisconsin’s 11 tribes and other subsistence fishers.

# Water
## Key Points
### Great Lakes Changes Will Affect Recreation and Infrastructure
Warming waters in the Great Lakes are impacting lake ecology, fisheries, and water-quality based recreation. Both increasing precipitation and drought are leading to extreme lake level fluctuations in Lake Superior and Lake Michigan that impact both habitats and structures built along the lakeshore.

# Water
## Key Points
### Mississippi River Seeing Impacts to Habitat
A wetter climate is increasing the volume of water flowing in the Mississippi River and impacting critical backwater habitat and recreational fishing opportunities.

# Water
## Solutions
Manage watersheds to reduce flood hazards and slow sediment and water movement in tributaries.
Invest in flood risk reduction practices and pre-disaster mitigation programs that help communities address local flood risks and avoid catastrophic losses.
Manage fisheries and make them more resilient to climate impacts by preventing overharvest, protecting productive populations, and preserving stronghold populations of brook trout and other important fisheries.
Conserve water and encourage water infiltration to reduce the impact of both droughts and floods.

June 9, 2014, 8:45 a.m. CT
Save this article and refer to it often!
June is Invasive Species Awareness Month in Wisconsin. Make a commitment to learning all you can about the plants and animals that threaten our native landscapes and water resources.
The state of Wisconsin, as well as several conservation groups, maintain wonderful online resources to help you navigate the confusing world of invasive species, as well as offering control measures, tips, and up-to-date information on the current status of many of these exotic invaders.
Listings of all of the current plants that are identified as either “prohibited” or “restricted” in our state are available. In addition, all of the proposed changes to the current invasive species rule, NR 40, are provided, along with contact information should you wish to let your voice be heard.
Here is a rundown of some of the best web resources available. Make time to explore each of them carefully to learn all you can about the invasive plants of our area.
Wisconsin DNR invasive species resources
The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources offers a great catalog of information on invasive plants at: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/invasives/
Here you will be able to link to resources to help you identify and control invasive plants, as well as report threatened areas, retailers that may be selling the plants and other observations.
Resources on the DNR site explore terrestrial invasives, as well as aquatic invasive plants, which threaten our waterways in more serious ways than most people ever consider.
Photographic quick tool to invasive species ID
Download and print a photographic guide to 64 of the most invasive terrestrial plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/files/pdf/pubs/fr/FR0464.pdf
This listing contains photos, latin name and common name of the most threatening plants to help you easily identify the plants that may be prowling around your area.
Invasive Species Rule NR 40
Helpful information and explanations of the current Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/classification.html

This rule serves as the law regarding invasive species in Wisconsin. As you may know, proposed changes are being considered and there is an open public comment period through June 30 to let your voice be heard. The above link contains contact information for comments, as well as information on two public hearings coming up this month on the proposed changes.
NR 40 plant listing
A printable listing of all invasive plants and animals currently covered under Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/documents/NR40ListsSep292010.pdf
Current NR 40 plant listing with photos and fact sheets
The DNR provides a wonderful listing of all plants currently covered under the invasive species rule, along with fact sheets containing control measures, all found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect
Proposed NR 40 additions
The DNR is proposing adding over 80 new plants to the NR 40 invasive species listing of regulated species. Find a listing of all of these plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsProposed#RegSelect
Wisconsin Invasive Species Council
In addition to the Wisconsin DNR resources, the Wisconsin Invasive Species Council provides a wealth of information on Invasive Species Awareness Month on their website found here: http://invasivespecies.wi.gov/awareness/
Invasive species awareness for children
Help educate your children on invasive species with the child-friendly information found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/org/caer/ce/eek/earth/aliens.htm
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
Another great resource for invasive plant information, including a working list of all invasive plants, with fact sheets, photos and more can be found here: http://ipaw.org.
This is a wonderful site and well worth the time to explore.
USDA national invasive information
The USDA offers a national website on invasive species here: http://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/index.shtml

GRASSED WATERWAY
Standards:

% of Mix   lbs/Acre  
Smooth bromegrass   20   4

Orchardgrass   20   2
2.  There shall be no state regulated invasive plants within the grassed waterway at any time during the agreement period.  
Information on regulated invasive plants and eradication methods are found at:
http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect
3.  Landowner shall contact Rock County Land Conservation Department (LCD), 608‐754‐6617 when an adequate forage plant  
density is established.  An adequate stand shall consist of species listed in standard #1 at a density of 10 forage plants per  
square foot.
Rock County LCD shall evaluate, document results and certify an adequate forage plant density has been established.
*Please note: no evaluations shall occur until after companion crop has been harvested and forage plant species have  
regrown to a height of 4 inches.

## [PDF page 102]
4.  Landowner may apply pesticides and fungicides according to federal and state approved label directions.

5.  Landowner may apply fertilizers not containing phosphorus if applied per University of Wisconsin publication A2809 which  
is found at:  http://learningstore.uwex.edu/assets/pdfs/A2809.pdf

6.  Landowner may harvest and remove the forage for agricultural production.

7.  Landowner may remove forage by mowing.  If wildlife production is desired, consider delaying mowing until after August 1.

8.  Landowner may remove mature forage using prescribed burning.  The prescribed burning should be completed by qualified  
personnel.  More information is found at:  http://www.prescribedfire.org/

9.  No livestock production shall occur within the grassed waterway at any time during the agreement period.

10.  If rills, gullies or other erosion or damage by machinery or herbicide occurs at any time during agreement period,  
landowner shall immediately repair and revegetate immediately.

11.  Lift tillage equipment when crossing waterway.  Avoid using waterways as a field access road, turn‐rows during tillage and  
cultivation operations.  Avoid crossing with heavy equipment when wet.
12.  Remove sediment deposits to maintain capacity of grassed waterway.

June 9, 2014, 8:45 a.m. CT
Save this article and refer to it often!
June is Invasive Species Awareness Month in Wisconsin. Make a commitment to learning all you can about the plants and animals that threaten our native landscapes and water resources.
The state of Wisconsin, as well as several conservation groups, maintain wonderful online resources to help you navigate the confusing world of invasive species, as well as offering control measures, tips, and up-to-date information on the current status of many of these exotic invaders.
Listings of all of the current plants that are identified as either “prohibited” or “restricted” in our state are available. In addition, all of the proposed changes to the current invasive species rule, NR 40, are provided, along with contact information should you wish to let your voice be heard.
Here is a rundown of some of the best web resources available. Make time to explore each of them carefully to learn all you can about the invasive plants of our area.
Wisconsin DNR invasive species resources
The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources offers a great catalog of information on invasive plants at: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/invasives/
Here you will be able to link to resources to help you identify and control invasive plants, as well as report threatened areas, retailers that may be selling the plants and other observations.
Resources on the DNR site explore terrestrial invasives, as well as aquatic invasive plants, which threaten our waterways in more serious ways than most people ever consider.
Photographic quick tool to invasive species ID
Download and print a photographic guide to 64 of the most invasive terrestrial plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/files/pdf/pubs/fr/FR0464.pdf
This listing contains photos, latin name and common name of the most threatening plants to help you easily identify the plants that may be prowling around your area.
Invasive Species Rule NR 40
Helpful information and explanations of the current Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/classification.html
texts.1:
This rule serves as the law regarding invasive species in Wisconsin. As you may know, proposed changes are being considered and there is an open public comment period through June 30 to let your voice be heard. The above link contains contact information for comments, as well as information on two public hearings coming up this month on the proposed changes.
NR 40 plant listing
A printable listing of all invasive plants and animals currently covered under Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/documents/NR40ListsSep292010.pdf
Current NR 40 plant listing with photos and fact sheets
The DNR provides a wonderful listing of all plants currently covered under the invasive species rule, along with fact sheets containing control measures, all found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect
Proposed NR 40 additions
The DNR is proposing adding over 80 new plants to the NR 40 invasive species listing of regulated species. Find a listing of all of these plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsProposed#RegSelect
Wisconsin Invasive Species Council
In addition to the Wisconsin DNR resources, the Wisconsin Invasive Species Council provides a wealth of information on Invasive Species Awareness Month on their website found here: http://invasivespecies.wi.gov/awareness/
Invasive species awareness for children
Help educate your children on invasive species with the child-friendly information found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/org/caer/ce/eek/earth/aliens.htm
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
Another great resource for invasive plant information, including a working list of all invasive plants, with fact sheets, photos and more can be found here: http://ipaw.org.
This is a wonderful site and well worth the time to explore.
USDA national invasive information
The USDA offers a national website on invasive species here: http://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/index.shtml
_— Rob Zimmer: 920-419-3734, yardmd@postcrescent.com_

Title: Yard MD blog: Where to go for invasive species help

June 9, 2014, 8:45 a.m. CT
Save this article and refer to it often!
June is Invasive Species Awareness Month in Wisconsin. Make a commitment to learning all you can about the plants and animals that threaten our native landscapes and water resources.
The state of Wisconsin, as well as several conservation groups, maintain wonderful online resources to help you navigate the confusing world of invasive species, as well as offering control measures, tips, and up-to-date information on the current status of many of these exotic invaders.
Listings of all of the current plants that are identified as either “prohibited” or “restricted” in our state are available. In addition, all of the proposed changes to the current invasive species rule, NR 40, are provided, along with contact information should you wish to let your voice be heard.
Here is a rundown of some of the best web resources available. Make time to explore each of them carefully to learn all you can about the invasive plants of our area.
Wisconsin DNR invasive species resources
The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources offers a great catalog of information on invasive plants at: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/invasives/
Here you will be able to link to resources to help you identify and control invasive plants, as well as report threatened areas, retailers that may be selling the plants and other observations.
Resources on the DNR site explore terrestrial invasives, as well as aquatic invasive plants, which threaten our waterways in more serious ways than most people ever consider.
Photographic quick tool to invasive species ID
Download and print a photographic guide to 64 of the most invasive terrestrial plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/files/pdf/pubs/fr/FR0464.pdf
This listing contains photos, latin name and common name of the most threatening plants to help you easily identify the plants that may be prowling around your area.
Invasive Species Rule NR 40
Helpful information and explanations of the current Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/classification.html

This rule serves as the law regarding invasive species in Wisconsin. As you may know, proposed changes are being considered and there is an open public comment period through June 30 to let your voice be heard. The above link contains contact information for comments, as well as information on two public hearings coming up this month on the proposed changes.
NR 40 plant listing
A printable listing of all invasive plants and animals currently covered under Invasive Species Rule NR 40 can be found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/documents/NR40ListsSep292010.pdf
Current NR 40 plant listing with photos and fact sheets
The DNR provides a wonderful listing of all plants currently covered under the invasive species rule, along with fact sheets containing control measures, all found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect
Proposed NR 40 additions
The DNR is proposing adding over 80 new plants to the NR 40 invasive species listing of regulated species. Find a listing of all of these plants here: http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsProposed#RegSelect
Wisconsin Invasive Species Council
In addition to the Wisconsin DNR resources, the Wisconsin Invasive Species Council provides a wealth of information on Invasive Species Awareness Month on their website found here: http://invasivespecies.wi.gov/awareness/
Invasive species awareness for children
Help educate your children on invasive species with the child-friendly information found here: http://dnr.wi.gov/org/caer/ce/eek/earth/aliens.htm
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
Another great resource for invasive plant information, including a working list of all invasive plants, with fact sheets, photos and more can be found here: http://ipaw.org.
This is a wonderful site and well worth the time to explore.
USDA national invasive information
The USDA offers a national website on invasive species here: http://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/index.shtml
_— Rob Zimmer: 920-419-3734, yardmd@postcrescent.com_

# Invasive Plant Species
Invasive species are non-native plants that cause damage to native ecosystems due to loss of diversity. This can be detrimental to local economies, recreation, and environmental health.
According to the WI DNR, approximately 42% of the species on the federal endangered species list or threatened endangered list are at risk primarily because of invasive species. The DNR provides A Field Guide to Invasive Plants in Wisconsin.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Reporting
Report any invasive species that you find to the WDNR.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Keep it Clean
If you transport a boat to a new body of water, be sure to properly inspect and check for stowaways such as Eurasian Watermilfoil and Zebra Mussels. These aquatic invasives tend to “hitch a ride” to new lakes. Make sure to drain all water from aquatic vehicles and remove all plants immediately after leaving a body of water.
If you are walking through land areas that already have invasive species, be sure to clean your clothes and equipment prior to leaving. This prevents seeds from attaching to you or your equipment and being transported to new areas.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Eradication of Invasives
There are many methods to properly remove invasive species if they infest your property. Some of these methods include mechanical, chemical, or biological removal. Mechanical removal most often includes hand-pulling plants or using a machine to do so. Chemical removal includes using an herbicide to kill the invasive species. Biological removal often includes introducing an animal to eat the undesired plants. Please do research prior to removing an invasive species from your property to ensure your own safety and that the species are properly removed so they will not return. It is important to know what type of plant you are dealing with- wild parsnip, as an example, can cause skin burning and irritation. Following proper eradication procedures for invasive plants is crucial to prevent the unintentional spread and to ensure that they do not grow back. The WDNR provides many resources on the removal of invasive species.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Disposal
Invasive plants should be removed and sealed in plastic bags to be sent to the landfill. Small bags can be placed in your green refuse cart and large bags can be disposed of at the Fitchburg Recycling Drop off site (2373 S. Fish Hatchery Rd) in the dumpster marked 'yardwaste bags, invasive plants and empty oil containers'.​
​Visit the DNR invasive species webpage for more information on identification and control at http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect ​
​

## Identification & Management Resources
Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WI DNR)
This website provides detailed information on the Wisconsin DNR's invasive species management strategies, laws pertaining to invasive species, and resources and educational materials they provide. These materials include find ID guides, NR 40 regulations, and species lists.
​
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
IPAW provides a map of all known Cooperative Weed Management Areas across Wisconsin, along with the IPAW List of Wisconsin Invasives, which details species impact levels and the types of disturbance that facilitate their spread.Midwest Invasive Plant Network (MIPN)
MIPN offers a variety of resources including fact sheets, links to other resources, and the Plant Control Database, an interactive tool designed to help you identify the most effective treatment method for the target species.

## Native Plant Alternatives


## Featured Resources
Midwest Invasive Species Information Network (MISIN)
MISIN provides fact sheets with background information, identification training modules,and educational resources for invasive species, as well as an easy-to-use platform to report invasive species and view maps of reported populations.
EDDMapS Reporting Tool
EDDMapS is a free, easy-to-use online tool to report invasive species in your area. Your reports help track infestations, prioritize management efforts, and protect natural areas across Wisconsin. EDDMapS is also available in the Apple and Android App Stores!
PlayCleanGo  
This is an outreach-focused campaign with tips and signage for recreationists to help in stopping the spread of invasives, both terrestrial and aquatic.Shoreland Restoration Plan
Langlade County provides a program showing plant options for your specific ecotype. Answer four simple questions for all of the areas of your property, and you'll be given a variety of plants you can use!
Manage Invasives in the Your ForestLumberjack RC&D was awarded a Landscape Scale Restoration grant from the United States Forest Service. Partners in this grant are TIP and WHIP. Our goal is to restore forest lands and to work with private landowners to help improve the health of their forests.

## FAQs and Quick Tips
TIP Coordinator, Brianna, controlling Japanese knotweed for a landowner.
**What species does TIP focus on?**
Our priorities include species on the WI DNR's Regulated Invasive Species List. We also work on emerging threats and support landowners with widespread species that are especially harmful. The presence of invasive species can vary by location, but buckthorn, garlic mustard, wild parsnip, and Japanese knotweed are some of the more aggressive and problematic species in the TIP region.  
**How do I report an invasive species?**
You can report sightings using apps like EDDMapS and MISIN, both linked above under "Featured Resources". You can also contact TIP directly via email or on our "Invasive Species" tab by sending us a photo or two, location information, and a brief description of what you observed. Reporting can also be done by emailing the WI DNR at [invasive.species@wisconsin.gov](mailto:invasive.species@wisconsin.gov) or completing a reporting form.
**I found an invasive plant in my yard. What should I do?**
Start by correctly identifying the plant using an app like Seek or iNaturalist, or contacting TIP or the DNR for assistance. Once identified, remove the plant using safe and appropriate methods, dispose of it properly, and consider replacing it with native species. TIP can advise you or help connect you with additional resources.  
**Can I request a site visit?**
Yes! Depending on staff availability and priority level, we can visit your property to identify invasive species, offer management recommendations, and help you plan next steps to control the species. You can contact us via phone, email, Facebook message, or through the reporting box or Google Form under "Invasive Species."
**Will TIP remove invasive species for me?**
In many cases, yes, especially if the species is prohibited. For work on private lands, we require a Landowner Participation Agreement on file which allows TIP to safely and legally conduct invasive species control on your property. While we cannot assist with _every_ infestation, we may provide removal, monitoring, and management recommendations when resources allow.
**Does TIP provide herbicide?**
We don't supply herbicide for personal use, but we may use it during TIP-organized treatments when appropriate. We're always happy to recommend safe, effective options and application tips for landowners treating invasive species on their own.
**Can I get involved?**

## FAQs and Quick Tips
Yes, definitely! You can sign up for our Mailing Listto receive updates and events from TIP, or you can become a TIP Volunteer. Volunteers of all ages are welcome, but youth must be supervised. You can also help spread awareness in your community by planting native species, practicing and promoting clean gear habits, or share TIP's events and updates on your own social media pages. If you have further questions, please call or email us - we're happy to help you, help us!
Installed boot brush in Menominee County.
**Tips from TIP:**
_Identify Invasives_
*   Look for common invasive species like garlic mustard (spring to early-summer), wild parsnip (summer), and common and glossy buckthorn (late-summer to fall). You can use apps like Seek, iNaturalist, or EDDMapS to help identify plants in your area.
_Practice Safe Outdoor Habits_
*   Wear long pants, closed-toe shoes, and gloves when you're outdoors looking for invasives. Always be sure to wear sunscreen during your time outside and to check for ticks after!
_Use Safe Removal Techniques_
*   Hand-pull small plants, make sure to remove the roots! Cut larger shrubs low and treat stumps when possible. You should bag all seedheads of plants to prevent the spread -**do not compost invasive plants**!
_Prevent the Spread of Invasives_
*   Clean your boots, bikes, and boats after use to ensure there aren't any invasive species debris stuck to you like seeds or small creatures. You should not transport firewood or any invasive plants. Choose to plant native species in your landscaping instead (resources above!)

## For Kids, Families, and Educators
TIP Coordinator, Abby, presenting at Pulaski Community Middle School.
Project Learning Tree
Project Learning Tree provides student pages, applications of STEM, reading resources, family activities, and so much more. Check out their website to begin learning about invasive species and other nature topics!
​
K-12 Activities and Lesson Plans
WI DNR has provided a few resources for students wanting to learn more about invasive species, both terrestrial and aquatic!
Games, Activities, and More!

# Invasive Plant Species
Invasive species are non-native plants that cause damage to native ecosystems due to loss of diversity. This can be detrimental to local economies, recreation, and environmental health.
According to the WI DNR, approximately 42% of the species on the federal endangered species list or threatened endangered list are at risk primarily because of invasive species. The DNR provides A Field Guide to Invasive Plants in Wisconsin.

### Reporting

texts.3:
# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Keep it Clean
If you transport a boat to a new body of water, be sure to properly inspect and check for stowaways such as Eurasian Watermilfoil and Zebra Mussels. These aquatic invasives tend to “hitch a ride” to new lakes. Make sure to drain all water from aquatic vehicles and remove all plants immediately after leaving a body of water.
If you are walking through land areas that already have invasive species, be sure to clean your clothes and equipment prior to leaving. This prevents seeds from attaching to you or your equipment and being transported to new areas.
texts.4:
# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Eradication of Invasives
There are many methods to properly remove invasive species if they infest your property. Some of these methods include mechanical, chemical, or biological removal. Mechanical removal most often includes hand-pulling plants or using a machine to do so. Chemical removal includes using an herbicide to kill the invasive species. Biological removal often includes introducing an animal to eat the undesired plants. Please do research prior to removing an invasive species from your property to ensure your own safety and that the species are properly removed so they will not return. It is important to know what type of plant you are dealing with- wild parsnip, as an example, can cause skin burning and irritation. Following proper eradication procedures for invasive plants is crucial to prevent the unintentional spread and to ensure that they do not grow back. The WDNR provides many resources on the removal of invasive species.
texts.5:
# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Disposal
Invasive plants should be removed and sealed in plastic bags to be sent to the landfill. Small bags can be placed in your green refuse cart and large bags can be disposed of at the Fitchburg Recycling Drop off site (2373 S. Fish Hatchery Rd) in the dumpster marked 'yardwaste bags, invasive plants and empty oil containers'.​
​Visit the DNR invasive species webpage for more information on identification and control at http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect ​
​

## Identification & Management Resources
Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WI DNR)
This website provides detailed information on the Wisconsin DNR's invasive species management strategies, laws pertaining to invasive species, and resources and educational materials they provide. These materials include find ID guides, NR 40 regulations, and species lists.
​
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
IPAW provides a map of all known Cooperative Weed Management Areas across Wisconsin, along with the IPAW List of Wisconsin Invasives, which details species impact levels and the types of disturbance that facilitate their spread.Midwest Invasive Plant Network (MIPN)
MIPN offers a variety of resources including fact sheets, links to other resources, and the Plant Control Database, an interactive tool designed to help you identify the most effective treatment method for the target species.
texts.2:
## Featured Resources
Midwest Invasive Species Information Network (MISIN)
MISIN provides fact sheets with background information, identification training modules,and educational resources for invasive species, as well as an easy-to-use platform to report invasive species and view maps of reported populations.
EDDMapS Reporting Tool
EDDMapS is a free, easy-to-use online tool to report invasive species in your area. Your reports help track infestations, prioritize management efforts, and protect natural areas across Wisconsin. EDDMapS is also available in the Apple and Android App Stores!
PlayCleanGo  
This is an outreach-focused campaign with tips and signage for recreationists to help in stopping the spread of invasives, both terrestrial and aquatic.Shoreland Restoration Plan
Langlade County provides a program showing plant options for your specific ecotype. Answer four simple questions for all of the areas of your property, and you'll be given a variety of plants you can use!
Manage Invasives in the Your ForestLumberjack RC&D was awarded a Landscape Scale Restoration grant from the United States Forest Service. Partners in this grant are TIP and WHIP. Our goal is to restore forest lands and to work with private landowners to help improve the health of their forests.
texts.3:
## FAQs and Quick Tips
TIP Coordinator, Brianna, controlling Japanese knotweed for a landowner.
**What species does TIP focus on?**
Our priorities include species on the WI DNR's Regulated Invasive Species List. We also work on emerging threats and support landowners with widespread species that are especially harmful. The presence of invasive species can vary by location, but buckthorn, garlic mustard, wild parsnip, and Japanese knotweed are some of the more aggressive and problematic species in the TIP region.  
**How do I report an invasive species?**
You can report sightings using apps like EDDMapS and MISIN, both linked above under "Featured Resources". You can also contact TIP directly via email or on our "Invasive Species" tab by sending us a photo or two, location information, and a brief description of what you observed. Reporting can also be done by emailing the WI DNR at [invasive.species@wisconsin.gov](mailto:invasive.species@wisconsin.gov) or completing a reporting form.
**I found an invasive plant in my yard. What should I do?**
Start by correctly identifying the plant using an app like Seek or iNaturalist, or contacting TIP or the DNR for assistance. Once identified, remove the plant using safe and appropriate methods, dispose of it properly, and consider replacing it with native species. TIP can advise you or help connect you with additional resources.  
**Can I request a site visit?**
Yes! Depending on staff availability and priority level, we can visit your property to identify invasive species, offer management recommendations, and help you plan next steps to control the species. You can contact us via phone, email, Facebook message, or through the reporting box or Google Form under "Invasive Species."
**Will TIP remove invasive species for me?**
In many cases, yes, especially if the species is prohibited. For work on private lands, we require a Landowner Participation Agreement on file which allows TIP to safely and legally conduct invasive species control on your property. While we cannot assist with _every_ infestation, we may provide removal, monitoring, and management recommendations when resources allow.
**Does TIP provide herbicide?**
We don't supply herbicide for personal use, but we may use it during TIP-organized treatments when appropriate. We're always happy to recommend safe, effective options and application tips for landowners treating invasive species on their own.
**Can I get involved?**
texts.4:
## FAQs and Quick Tips
Yes, definitely! You can sign up for our Mailing Listto receive updates and events from TIP, or you can become a TIP Volunteer. Volunteers of all ages are welcome, but youth must be supervised. You can also help spread awareness in your community by planting native species, practicing and promoting clean gear habits, or share TIP's events and updates on your own social media pages. If you have further questions, please call or email us - we're happy to help you, help us!
Installed boot brush in Menominee County.
**Tips from TIP:**
_Identify Invasives_
*   Look for common invasive species like garlic mustard (spring to early-summer), wild parsnip (summer), and common and glossy buckthorn (late-summer to fall). You can use apps like Seek, iNaturalist, or EDDMapS to help identify plants in your area.
_Practice Safe Outdoor Habits_
*   Wear long pants, closed-toe shoes, and gloves when you're outdoors looking for invasives. Always be sure to wear sunscreen during your time outside and to check for ticks after!
_Use Safe Removal Techniques_
*   Hand-pull small plants, make sure to remove the roots! Cut larger shrubs low and treat stumps when possible. You should bag all seedheads of plants to prevent the spread -**do not compost invasive plants**!
_Prevent the Spread of Invasives_
*   Clean your boots, bikes, and boats after use to ensure there aren't any invasive species debris stuck to you like seeds or small creatures. You should not transport firewood or any invasive plants. Choose to plant native species in your landscaping instead (resources above!)

# Invasive Plant Species
Invasive species are non-native plants that cause damage to native ecosystems due to loss of diversity. This can be detrimental to local economies, recreation, and environmental health.
According to the WI DNR, approximately 42% of the species on the federal endangered species list or threatened endangered list are at risk primarily because of invasive species. The DNR provides A Field Guide to Invasive Plants in Wisconsin.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Reporting
Report any invasive species that you find to the WDNR.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Keep it Clean
If you transport a boat to a new body of water, be sure to properly inspect and check for stowaways such as Eurasian Watermilfoil and Zebra Mussels. These aquatic invasives tend to “hitch a ride” to new lakes. Make sure to drain all water from aquatic vehicles and remove all plants immediately after leaving a body of water.
If you are walking through land areas that already have invasive species, be sure to clean your clothes and equipment prior to leaving. This prevents seeds from attaching to you or your equipment and being transported to new areas.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Eradication of Invasives
There are many methods to properly remove invasive species if they infest your property. Some of these methods include mechanical, chemical, or biological removal. Mechanical removal most often includes hand-pulling plants or using a machine to do so. Chemical removal includes using an herbicide to kill the invasive species. Biological removal often includes introducing an animal to eat the undesired plants. Please do research prior to removing an invasive species from your property to ensure your own safety and that the species are properly removed so they will not return. It is important to know what type of plant you are dealing with- wild parsnip, as an example, can cause skin burning and irritation. Following proper eradication procedures for invasive plants is crucial to prevent the unintentional spread and to ensure that they do not grow back. The WDNR provides many resources on the removal of invasive species.

# Invasive Plant Species
## How You Can Stop the Spread
### Disposal
Invasive plants should be removed and sealed in plastic bags to be sent to the landfill. Small bags can be placed in your green refuse cart and large bags can be disposed of at the Fitchburg Recycling Drop off site (2373 S. Fish Hatchery Rd) in the dumpster marked 'yardwaste bags, invasive plants and empty oil containers'.​
​Visit the DNR invasive species webpage for more information on identification and control at http://dnr.wi.gov/topic/Invasives/species.asp?filterBy=Terrestrial&filterVal=Y&catVal=PlantsReg#RegSelect ​

## Identification & Management Resources
Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WI DNR)
This website provides detailed information on the Wisconsin DNR's invasive species management strategies, laws pertaining to invasive species, and resources and educational materials they provide. These materials include find ID guides, NR 40 regulations, and species lists.
​
Invasive Plant Association of Wisconsin (IPAW)
IPAW provides a map of all known Cooperative Weed Management Areas across Wisconsin, along with the IPAW List of Wisconsin Invasives, which details species impact levels and the types of disturbance that facilitate their spread.Midwest Invasive Plant Network (MIPN)
MIPN offers a variety of resources including fact sheets, links to other resources, and the Plant Control Database, an interactive tool designed to help you identify the most effective treatment method for the target species.

## Native Plant Alternatives


## Featured Resources
Midwest Invasive Species Information Network (MISIN)
MISIN provides fact sheets with background information, identification training modules,and educational resources for invasive species, as well as an easy-to-use platform to report invasive species and view maps of reported populations.
EDDMapS Reporting Tool
EDDMapS is a free, easy-to-use online tool to report invasive species in your area. Your reports help track infestations, prioritize management efforts, and protect natural areas across Wisconsin. EDDMapS is also available in the Apple and Android App Stores!
PlayCleanGo  
This is an outreach-focused campaign with tips and signage for recreationists to help in stopping the spread of invasives, both terrestrial and aquatic.Shoreland Restoration Plan
Langlade County provides a program showing plant options for your specific ecotype. Answer four simple questions for all of the areas of your property, and you'll be given a variety of plants you can use!
Manage Invasives in the Your ForestLumberjack RC&D was awarded a Landscape Scale Restoration grant from the United States Forest Service. Partners in this grant are TIP and WHIP. Our goal is to restore forest lands and to work with private landowners to help improve the health of their forests.

## FAQs and Quick Tips
TIP Coordinator, Brianna, controlling Japanese knotweed for a landowner.
**What species does TIP focus on?**
Our priorities include species on the WI DNR's Regulated Invasive Species List. We also work on emerging threats and support landowners with widespread species that are especially harmful. The presence of invasive species can vary by location, but buckthorn, garlic mustard, wild parsnip, and Japanese knotweed are some of the more aggressive and problematic species in the TIP region.  
**How do I report an invasive species?**
You can report sightings using apps like EDDMapS and MISIN, both linked above under "Featured Resources". You can also contact TIP directly via email or on our "Invasive Species" tab by sending us a photo or two, location information, and a brief description of what you observed. Reporting can also be done by emailing the WI DNR at [invasive.species@wisconsin.gov](mailto:invasive.species@wisconsin.gov) or completing a reporting form.
**I found an invasive plant in my yard. What should I do?**
Start by correctly identifying the plant using an app like Seek or iNaturalist, or contacting TIP or the DNR for assistance. Once identified, remove the plant using safe and appropriate methods, dispose of it properly, and consider replacing it with native species. TIP can advise you or help connect you with additional resources.  
**Can I request a site visit?**
Yes! Depending on staff availability and priority level, we can visit your property to identify invasive species, offer management recommendations, and help you plan next steps to control the species. You can contact us via phone, email, Facebook message, or through the reporting box or Google Form under "Invasive Species."
**Will TIP remove invasive species for me?**
In many cases, yes, especially if the species is prohibited. For work on private lands, we require a Landowner Participation Agreement on file which allows TIP to safely and legally conduct invasive species control on your property. While we cannot assist with _every_ infestation, we may provide removal, monitoring, and management recommendations when resources allow.
**Does TIP provide herbicide?**
We don't supply herbicide for personal use, but we may use it during TIP-organized treatments when appropriate. We're always happy to recommend safe, effective options and application tips for landowners treating invasive species on their own.
**Can I get involved?**

## FAQs and Quick Tips
Yes, definitely! You can sign up for our Mailing Listto receive updates and events from TIP, or you can become a TIP Volunteer. Volunteers of all ages are welcome, but youth must be supervised. You can also help spread awareness in your community by planting native species, practicing and promoting clean gear habits, or share TIP's events and updates on your own social media pages. If you have further questions, please call or email us - we're happy to help you, help us!
Installed boot brush in Menominee County.
**Tips from TIP:**
_Identify Invasives_
*   Look for common invasive species like garlic mustard (spring to early-summer), wild parsnip (summer), and common and glossy buckthorn (late-summer to fall). You can use apps like Seek, iNaturalist, or EDDMapS to help identify plants in your area.
_Practice Safe Outdoor Habits_
*   Wear long pants, closed-toe shoes, and gloves when you're outdoors looking for invasives. Always be sure to wear sunscreen during your time outside and to check for ticks after!
_Use Safe Removal Techniques_
*   Hand-pull small plants, make sure to remove the roots! Cut larger shrubs low and treat stumps when possible. You should bag all seedheads of plants to prevent the spread -**do not compost invasive plants**!
_Prevent the Spread of Invasives_
*   Clean your boots, bikes, and boats after use to ensure there aren't any invasive species debris stuck to you like seeds or small creatures. You should not transport firewood or any invasive plants. Choose to plant native species in your landscaping instead (resources above!)

## For Kids, Families, and Educators
TIP Coordinator, Abby, presenting at Pulaski Community Middle School.
Project Learning Tree
Project Learning Tree provides student pages, applications of STEM, reading resources, family activities, and so much more. Check out their website to begin learning about invasive species and other nature topics!
​
K-12 Activities and Lesson Plans
WI DNR has provided a few resources for students wanting to learn more about invasive species, both terrestrial and aquatic!
Games, Activities, and More!
The USDA's National Invasive Species Information Center lists numerous resources for games, activities, videos, coloring books, and more. They also provide resources for educators, here! Check out their website for other outreach materials and campaigns.
Invasive Species Go-Around_(for educators)_
National Park Service provides a laid-out activity for educators of 6th - 8th graders. The activity allows students to focus on an invasive species and present the information to their classmates.Environmental Education Events_(for educators)_
Educators! Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction provides a number of events that helps teachers incorporate the environment into their instruction. From math in the forest to connecting urban area students to nature - check it out!
